question: What is an Expository sermon? Examine the advantages of an Expository sermon.
idealAnswer: Preachers who preach expository sermons select a paragraph of Scripture, discover the theme from the passage and develop it point by point using evidence from the chosen paragraphs. Here the preacher uses the sermon to expose what the meaning of the Scripture is. When preaching expository sermons one needs to study the passage until its insight is clear to him or her, and allow the content of the passage, and the background surrounding it, to determine its treatment. The expository sermon, like the textual sermon, takes its subject and main points from a particular text, but unlike the textual sermon it also takes its sub-points from the immediate text; references to other texts may occur, but they are used only to support, elaborate or confirm what is already evident in the immediate text. A sermon is not expository merely because it addresses a subject in the Bible or because it cites numerous Scriptures: the true expository sermon discloses the thoughts of the author, covers the range of the passage, and applies its truths to the lives of the listeners. The advantages of expository preaching are several. The main advantage is that it gives the hope of possibly covering the entire Bible, for an expositor who does not pick and choose favourite passages but expounds the Bible bit by bit in a sequential order may hopefully cover the whole Bible in a given period of time, no matter how long it takes. Secondly, the preacher will always have a sermon subject to preach on; very few preachers have preached through the entire Bible in their lifetime or with one congregation, and those who finish with the same congregation will find many new faces have come in, so they can start all over again. Thirdly, expository preaching focuses the hearer's attention on the Scripture as the source of authority and teaching. Fourthly, the preacher does not expound just a great book, a poem, a political passage, or his personal opinion; rather he or she concentrates on the authoritative word of God. Finally, the expository sermon demands integrity on the part of the preacher.

subject: LIT
question: Define a sermon and explain what the following words mean when used to describe a sermon: prophetic, kerygmatic, didactic, and therapeutic.
idealAnswer: Preaching the sermon is essentially telling the Good News to people; this Good News is about God, or from God. A sermon is therefore not a personal view about current events, whether social or political, nor even about current theological issues, but the word of God as contained in the Scriptures, delivered with the aim of bringing home its saving and liberating truth to the hearers and enabling them to understand that truth in relation to their lives. This is not accomplished by the preacher but by the Holy Spirit, who uses the preacher as an agent to bring the truth to the people. Bernard Manning sees preaching the sermon as a “manifestation of the Incarnate Word, from the written word, by the spoken word”, while Bultmann defines preaching as “the communication of Biblical truth by man to man with the explicit purpose of eliciting behavioural change”. Unlike an address, a sermon is geared towards eliciting behavioural change and is thus aligned with decision-making. Four words are used to describe the sermon. It is prophetic in that preaching should point out what things are wrong and how to remedy them, and is further aimed at teaching those who do not know the way of God to know it. It is kerygmatic in that its purpose is the proclaiming of the Gospel. It is didactic in that its purpose is teaching. And it is therapeutic in that it is aimed at healing the broken spirit and the broken society. These purposes together show why the uniqueness of sermons calls for a distinctive way of preparation, and why the preacher, who preaches best with his lifestyle, must be an imitator of Christ, a person of deep piety and affection for others.

subject: LIT
question: What is prayer? Discuss the content of a prayer.
idealAnswer: Prayer is a conversation or communication with God. It is the means by which we link up our souls with the Spirit of God and convey our heart's desires and concerns to Him. Real prayer is expressing our devotion to our heavenly Father and inviting Him to talk to us as we talk to Him. It is the intercourse of the soul with God, not only in contemplation or meditation but also in direct address to Him, and it may be oral or mental, occasional or constant, extempore or formal. Throughout the Bible prayer is described variously as calling upon the name of the Lord, beseeching the Lord, pouring out the soul before the Lord, crying to heaven, seeking unto God and making supplication, drawing near to God and approaching God's throne of grace. Although prayer cannot be reduced to a mere formula, there are certain basic elements that should be included in our communication with God; this formula is popularly known as CATS or ACTS — Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication. To adore God is to worship and praise Him, to honour and exalt Him in our heart and mind and with our lips; we need not begin our prayer by placing a tall list of requests before God, for prayer is interaction with God and not a presentation of requests, and adoration should be the entry point of our prayer. When our discipline of prayer begins with adoration, the Holy Spirit has opportunity to reveal any sin in our life that needs to be confessed; confession of sins must be sincere and specific, and must culminate in repentance and change. Thanksgiving is the expression of gratitude or appreciation to God, for who He is and for the benefits we enjoy because we belong to Him; it enables us to recognise that He controls all things, not just the blessings but the problems and adversities as well. Supplication includes petition for our own needs and intercession for others. Petition is asking God for personal things in prayer, while intercession is prayer for others — for our families, neighbours, those in authority and the nation, and for the salvation of souls. For the preacher, intercession is an integral part of the ministry, for a preacher who does not pray for those he or she preaches to has an incomplete and unfulfilled ministry.

question: Outline the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana and examine its relevance.
idealAnswer: The outline of the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana runs as follows: Call to Worship; Introit; Hymn; Prayer; Hymn or Lyric; The Ministry of the Word; The Old Testament; The Epistle; Te Deum; The Gospel Reading; Affirmation of Faith; Hymn; Sermon; Invitation to Christian Discipleship; Announcements; Tithes and Offertory; Hymn; and Benediction and Dismissal. Its relevance may be examined item by item. The Call to Worship is a way of calling the congregation's attention to the fact that the service is about to begin, after which the Choir, Singing Band and Clergy process; where the procession comes first, the liturgist may join the call to worship and welcome as one item after the introit. The Introit is sung in preparation for the continuation of the worship service after the procession by the choir. The Affirmation of Faith acts as a yardstick of correct belief, the Apostles' Creed being said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days, and by it Methodists affirm the doctrine of the Trinity. The place given to Lyrics helps to control the spontaneous singing of lyrics, while still allowing the preacher to accept those that are relevant to the sermon. The Response and Dedication, or altar call, is where people give or rededicate their lives to Christ, or seek corporate assistance in prayer, in response to the Word preached, and is the appropriate time for ministry in healing, deliverance or the gifts of the Spirit, and for testimony sharing. The Dismissal with Blessing belongs to the clergy, and whenever a minister is present the local preacher must give him or her the first option to pronounce the benediction. Above all, the order of service is mainly a guideline: it is there to guide us in the conduct of worship but not to pin us down, and there should always be reasonable and cautious flexibility. The Te Deum, for instance, may be varied with other canticles, a shorter canticle being sung where time must be saved, though some canticles are occasion specific — it is always appropriate to sing the Magnificat during Christmas.

subject: LIT
question: What is Pentecost? Examine the importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's Calendar.
idealAnswer: In Judaism, Pentecost was a harvest festival which was also known as the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of First Fruits. The descent of the Holy Spirit recorded in the Book of Acts took place at the Jewish Pentecost, and this made Christians fix their celebration of the pouring down of the Holy Spirit on the fiftieth day after Easter, that is, the seventh Sunday after Easter. It was a day of universal rejoicing, and as Tertullian records, “we spent our time in all exaltation”. The importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's calendar may be seen in several ways. St. Athanasius calls it “Magna Dominica”, the “Great Sunday”, and consequently neither fasting nor kneeling was allowed during its celebration. Pentecost Sunday is also called White Sunday or Whitsunday, possibly in reference to the white robes worn by catechumens and others who were baptised on that day; an alternative derivation is from the word “wit” or “wisdom”, which implies that it was the day the Apostles were filled with wisdom from God by the Holy Spirit. The sanctuary colour of Pentecost Sunday is red, the colour of the Church. The red symbolises the Fire of Pentecost as well as that of the Apostles and other disciples of Jesus who were gathered in the Upper Room for the empowerment from God to preach the gospel to other nations.

subject: LIT
question: Discuss a Textual Sermon and its advantages.
idealAnswer: In textual sermons the preacher takes a few verses, a verse, or even a part of a verse from the Bible. The preacher discovers the theme of the verse in context and preaches on it in his own words. In the textual sermon both the subject and the main points are based on ideas in the text, but, unlike the expository sermon, the development of the main ideas comes from sources outside of the immediate text. This sermon looks to the text to bring out the meaning, and uses the “hook-book-look-and-took” method: something is used to hook the audience, such as an interesting story that would bring people to think about the sermon; the book is turning to the Scripture; look discusses what that Scripture is saying; and the took is what each person should take away from the sermon. It is almost a combination of the narrative and expository sermons. A textual sermon is generally good for preaching to audiences with short attention spans such as children and the elderly, for preaching at occasions other than church services such as banquets and funerals, and for preaching series on “Great Bible Texts” or “Favourite Bible Verses”. Its advantages are these. First, a textual sermon is a great technique for bringing the actual words of the Bible before the hearers, giving Divine authority to the message. Secondly, since the text is short it will be easier to remember or memorise, so the preacher can easily make constant reference to the text many times during the sermon. Thirdly, the preacher who employs the textual method deals with distinctively Scriptural themes that come right out of the text, so that a well-constructed textual sermon is much more intimately in contact with the text, drawing from it not only the subject treated but all the leading thoughts of the treatment. Finally, it gives ample opportunity for variety, freshness and originality.

question: What is an Expository sermon? Examine the advantages of an Expository Sermon.
idealAnswer: Preachers who preach expository sermons select a paragraph of Scripture, discover the theme from the passage and develop it point by point using evidence from the chosen paragraphs. Here the preacher uses the sermon to expose what the meaning of the Scripture is. When preaching expository sermons one needs to study the passage until its insight is clear to him or her, and allow the content of the passage, and the background surrounding it, to determine its treatment. The expository sermon, like the textual sermon, takes its subject and main points from a particular text, but unlike the textual sermon it also takes its sub-points from the immediate text; references to other texts may occur, but they are used only to support, elaborate or confirm what is already evident in the immediate text. A sermon is not expository merely because it addresses a subject in the Bible or because it cites numerous Scriptures: the true expository sermon discloses the thoughts of the author, covers the range of the passage, and applies its truths to the lives of the listeners. The advantages of expository preaching are several. The main advantage is that it gives the hope of possibly covering the entire Bible, for an expositor who does not pick and choose favourite passages but expounds the Bible bit by bit in a sequential order may hopefully cover the whole Bible in a given period of time, no matter how long it takes. Secondly, the preacher will always have a sermon subject to preach on; very few preachers have preached through the entire Bible in their lifetime or with one congregation, and those who finish with the same congregation will find many new faces have come in, so they can start all over again. Thirdly, expository preaching focuses the hearer's attention on the Scripture as the source of authority and teaching. Fourthly, the preacher does not expound just a great book, a poem, a political passage, or his personal opinion; rather he or she concentrates on the authoritative word of God. Finally, the expository sermon demands integrity on the part of the preacher.

question: What is a creed? Write short notes on the Apostle's Creed.
idealAnswer: A creed is a statement of faith. The purpose of a creed is to act as a yardstick of correct belief. The creeds of Christianity have been drawn up at times of conflict about doctrine, and the acceptance or rejection of a creed serves to distinguish believers and deniers of a particular doctrine or set of doctrines. For that reason a creed was called in Greek a sumbolon, meaning half of a broken object which, when placed together with the other half, verified the bearer's identity; the Greek word passed through the Latin symbolum into the English symbol, which later took on the meaning of an outward sign of something. Creeds, as statements of faith, confirm the faithful in their faith, thus strengthening their corporate unity, and they should endorse what is at the core of the Christian faith as well as of the life of the wider community whose vicissitudes raise questions for the believer. The Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed are the ones commonly used among Ghanaian Methodists in affirming our faith, the Apostles' Creed being said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days. The Apostles' Creed is the basic creed of the Reformed churches. It is a statement of Christian belief and is widely used by a number of Christian denominations for both liturgical and catechetical purposes. It appears to have been originally formulated as a refutation of Gnosticism, an early heresy, and this can be seen in almost every phrase: for example, the creed states that Christ Jesus was born, suffered and died on the cross, which is a statement directly against the heretical teaching that Christ only appeared to become man and did not truly suffer and die but only appeared to do so. The Apostles' Creed, as well as other baptismal creeds, is esteemed as an example of the apostles' teachings and a defence of the Gospel of Christ. It does not, however, address some Christological issues defined in the Nicene and other Christian creeds; it thus says nothing explicitly about the divinity of either Jesus or of the Holy Spirit.

question: What is prayer? Discuss the content of a prayer.
idealAnswer: Prayer is a conversation or communication with God. It is the means by which we link up our souls with the Spirit of God and convey our heart's desires and concerns to Him. Real prayer is expressing our devotion to our heavenly Father and inviting Him to talk to us as we talk to Him. It is the intercourse of the soul with God, not only in contemplation or meditation but also in direct address to Him, and it may be oral or mental, occasional or constant, extempore or formal. Throughout the Bible prayer is described variously as calling upon the name of the Lord, beseeching the Lord, pouring out the soul before the Lord, crying to heaven, seeking unto God and making supplication, drawing near to God and approaching God's throne of grace. Although prayer cannot be reduced to a mere formula, there are certain basic elements that should be included in our communication with God; this formula is popularly known as CATS or ACTS — Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication. To adore God is to worship and praise Him, to honour and exalt Him in our heart and mind and with our lips; we need not begin our prayer by placing a tall list of requests before God, for prayer is interaction with God and not a presentation of requests, and adoration should be the entry point of our prayer. When our discipline of prayer begins with adoration, the Holy Spirit has opportunity to reveal any sin in our life that needs to be confessed; confession of sins must be sincere and specific, and must culminate in repentance and change. Thanksgiving is the expression of gratitude or appreciation to God, for who He is and for the benefits we enjoy because we belong to Him; it enables us to recognise that He controls all things, not just the blessings but the problems and adversities as well. Supplication includes petition for our own needs and intercession for others. Petition is asking God for personal things in prayer, while intercession is prayer for others — for our families, neighbours, those in authority and the nation, and for the salvation of souls. For the preacher, intercession is an integral part of the ministry, for a preacher who does not pray for those he or she preaches to has an incomplete and unfulfilled ministry.

question: Outline the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana and mention three relevance of the order.
idealAnswer: The outline of the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana runs as follows: Call to Worship; Introit; Hymn; Prayer; Hymn or Lyric; The Ministry of the Word; The Old Testament; The Epistle; Te Deum; The Gospel Reading; Affirmation of Faith; Hymn; Sermon; Invitation to Christian Discipleship; Announcements; Tithes and Offertory; Hymn; and Benediction and Dismissal. Three points of relevance may be mentioned. First, the order is mainly a guideline: it is there to guide us in the conduct of worship but not to pin us down, so that there should always be reasonable and cautious flexibility — the Te Deum, for instance, may be varied with other canticles, and where time must be saved a shorter canticle such as Canticle 6 may be sung, though some canticles are occasion specific and it is always appropriate to sing the Magnificat during Christmas. Secondly, particular items carry a particular purpose: the Call to Worship calls the congregation's attention to the fact that the service is about to begin, after which the Choir, Singing Band and Clergy process, while the Introit is sung in preparation for the continuation of the worship service after the procession; and the Affirmation of Faith acts as a yardstick of correct belief, the Apostles' Creed being said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days. Thirdly, the new order gives a specific place to items which had previously been spontaneous or neglected: it provides a specific place for lyrics, which helps to control the spontaneous ones while allowing those relevant to the sermon; and it makes room for the Response and Dedication, the altar call at which people give or rededicate their lives to Christ or seek corporate assistance in prayer in response to the Word preached, and the appropriate time for ministry in healing, deliverance and the gifts of the Spirit and for testimony sharing. Finally, the Dismissal with Blessing belongs to the clergy, and whenever a minister is present the local preacher must give him or her the first option to pronounce the benediction.

question: What is Pentecost? Examine the importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's Calendar.
idealAnswer: In Judaism, Pentecost was a harvest festival which was also known as the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of First Fruits. The descent of the Holy Spirit recorded in the Book of Acts took place at the Jewish Pentecost, and this made Christians fix their celebration of the pouring down of the Holy Spirit on the fiftieth day after Easter, that is, the seventh Sunday after Easter. It was a day of universal rejoicing, and as Tertullian records, “we spent our time in all exaltation”. The importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's calendar may be seen in several ways. St. Athanasius calls it “Magna Dominica”, the “Great Sunday”, and consequently neither fasting nor kneeling was allowed during its celebration. Pentecost Sunday is also called White Sunday or Whitsunday, possibly in reference to the white robes worn by catechumens and others who were baptised on that day; an alternative derivation is from the word “wit” or “wisdom”, which implies that it was the day the Apostles were filled with wisdom from God by the Holy Spirit. The sanctuary colour of Pentecost Sunday is red, the colour of the Church. The red symbolises the Fire of Pentecost as well as that of the Apostles and other disciples of Jesus who were gathered in the Upper Room for the empowerment from God to preach the gospel to other nations.

subject: LIT
question: Discuss the Manners that affect sermon delivery.
idealAnswer: After all the spiritual and physical preparation needed in the work of the preacher, one of the important tasks is how to deliver the sermon, for a preacher may write a very good sermon while the effectiveness or the achievement of the desired end of changing lives is largely determined by the delivery. The issues that affect sermon delivery include the appearance of the preacher and his or her body language, and other manners such as the tone of the preacher and his eye contact. As to appearance, the preacher's appearance has a major impact on the congregation, and the dressing must be decent; while modesty is necessary, it is not good to go to the pulpit shabbily dressed in the name of modesty, and depending on the social status of the congregation the dressing should be generally acceptable and neither offensive nor expensive. The preacher must avoid dresses that draw attention to the preacher rather than the message, and must look cheerful, healthy and fit. As to posture, the preacher must be mindful of how he or she carries himself in the pulpit: be yourself and imitate no one except Christ, be natural in voice and style, and do not put your hands in your pocket or on your waist, for it carries a wrong impression; the preacher should preach with passion, since a passionate preacher is more likely to make a positive impact than one emotionally detached from the message. As to gesture, the preacher may motion the hands, the head and other parts of the body to express or stress points, but this should be done with care; a microphone should be held in the left hand so that the right may be used to stress points, remembering that in some cultural settings using the left hand to talk to people is not acceptable, and the preacher should not be glued to words like Praise the Lord, Halleluiah and Amen just for the sake of it. As to tone, the preacher must check the tone of the voice and of the message; the gospel is a message of joy and happiness and the preacher must not sound too gloomy even when preaching on sin and repentance, and while some points may need a loud voice, it should not be the preacher's habit to shout — one should be heard without shouting, speaking clearly and confidently. The preacher must also involve the congregation, chiefly by calculated eye contact, consciously looking round to all corners of the chapel, and by verbally involving the people, leaving the ends of some quotations to be completed by them; notes may be consulted but staying too glued to them detaches the preacher from the people, and since the average listening capacity spans between ten and twenty-five minutes the preacher must be mindful of time. Finally, the preacher must know how to end the sermon: ending does not necessarily mean reaching the written conclusion or saying everything in the notes, and the preacher should be sensitive to the Holy Spirit, the time spent, the mood of the listeners and whether the peak of delivery has been reached — the peak being the point where anything more said brings down the excitement and joy of the listeners — and when these signs show, raise a song, repeat the text or theme, say a prayer and end there.

idealAnswer: Preachers who preach expository sermons select a paragraph of Scripture, discover the theme from the passage and develop it point by point using evidence from the chosen paragraphs. Here the preacher uses the sermon to expose what the meaning of the Scripture is, studying the passage until its insight is clear and allowing the content of the passage, and the background surrounding it, to determine its treatment. Like the textual sermon it takes its subject and main points from a particular text, but unlike the textual sermon it also takes its sub-points from the immediate text; references to other texts are used only to support, elaborate or confirm what is already evident there. The advantages are these. The main advantage is that it gives the hope of possibly covering the entire Bible, for an expositor who does not pick and choose favourite passages but expounds the Bible bit by bit in sequential order may hopefully cover the whole Bible in a given period of time. Secondly, the preacher will always have a sermon subject to preach on. Thirdly, expository preaching focuses the hearer's attention on the Scripture as the source of authority and teaching. Fourthly, the preacher does not expound just a great book, a poem, a political passage or his personal opinion, but concentrates on the authoritative word of God. Finally, the expository sermon demands integrity on the part of the preacher. The disadvantages are equally clear. The main disadvantage is that expository preaching covers many topics and necessitates often lengthy diversions into other passages for clarification; it does not allow for detailed coverage of a particular topic when only a specific text is covered, so that in order to address the context and content properly the preacher does become topical. Secondly, the expository sermon is a time-consuming task, and most expository preachers will never cover the entire Bible in their lifetime. Thirdly, Exegesis — the art of critically analysing or interpreting the passage, which must be done honestly — may give way to Eisegesis, the “art” of reading preconceived opinions into the text, so that the preacher forces out of the passage what he already wants to say. Finally, the expositor may wander from the text, departing from true exposition, stretching and straining it to draw lessons it was never intended to teach; thus, instead of exposing the passage, the preacher may rather exploit it. A further danger is that the expositor may fail to proceed from interpretation to application and so end up producing an expository lesson, which aims only at the mind, instead of an expository sermon, which also seeks to change the behaviour of the listeners.

subject: LIT
question: Define a sermon and explain what the following words mean when used to describe a sermon: prophetic, kerygmatic, didactic, and therapeutic.
idealAnswer: Preaching the sermon is essentially telling the Good News to people; this Good News is about God, or from God. A sermon is therefore not a personal view about current events, whether social or political, nor even about current theological issues, but the word of God as contained in the Scriptures, delivered with the aim of bringing home its saving and liberating truth to the hearers and enabling them to understand that truth in relation to their lives. This is not accomplished by the preacher but by the Holy Spirit, who uses the preacher as an agent to bring the truth to the people. Bernard Manning sees preaching the sermon as a “manifestation of the Incarnate Word, from the written word, by the spoken word”, while Bultmann defines preaching as “the communication of Biblical truth by man to man with the explicit purpose of eliciting behavioural change”. Unlike an address, a sermon is geared towards eliciting behavioural change and is thus aligned with decision-making. Four words describe the sermon. It is prophetic in that preaching should point out what things are wrong and how to remedy them, and is further aimed at teaching those who do not know the way of God to know it. It is kerygmatic in that its purpose is the proclaiming of the Gospel. It is didactic in that its purpose is teaching. And it is therapeutic in that it is aimed at healing the broken spirit and the broken society. These purposes together show why the uniqueness of sermons calls for a distinctive way of preparation, and why the preacher, who preaches best with his lifestyle, must be an imitator of Christ.

subject: LIT
question: What is prayer? Discuss the content of a prayer.
idealAnswer: Prayer is a conversation or communication with God. It is the means by which we link up our souls with the Spirit of God and convey our heart's desires and concerns to Him. Real prayer is expressing our devotion to our heavenly Father and inviting Him to talk to us as we talk to Him. It is the intercourse of the soul with God, not only in contemplation or meditation but also in direct address to Him, and it may be oral or mental, occasional or constant, extempore or formal. Throughout the Bible prayer is described variously as calling upon the name of the Lord, beseeching the Lord, pouring out the soul before the Lord, crying to heaven, seeking unto God and making supplication, and approaching God's throne of grace. Although prayer cannot be reduced to a mere formula, there are certain basic elements that should be included in our communication with God; this formula is popularly known as CATS or ACTS — Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication. To adore God is to worship and praise Him, to honour and exalt Him in our heart and mind and with our lips; we need not begin our prayer by placing a tall list of requests before God, for prayer is interaction with God and not a presentation of requests, and adoration should be the entry point of our prayer. When our discipline of prayer begins with adoration, the Holy Spirit has opportunity to reveal any sin in our life that needs to be confessed; confession of sins must be sincere and specific, and must culminate in repentance and change. Thanksgiving is the expression of gratitude or appreciation to God for who He is and for the benefits we enjoy because we belong to Him; Psalm 136 makes a tall list of what we must thank God for, because His mercy endures forever. Supplication includes petition for our own needs and intercession for others: petition is asking God for personal things in prayer, while intercession is prayer for others — for family, neighbours, those in authority and the nation, and for the salvation of souls. For the preacher, intercession is an integral part of the ministry, for a preacher who does not pray for those he or she preaches to has an incomplete and unfulfilled ministry.

chapter: THE METHODIST SUNDAY MORNING ORDER OF SERVICE
question: Outline the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana and examine its relevance.
idealAnswer: The outline of the new order for Sunday Morning Worship of the Methodist Church Ghana runs as follows: Call to Worship; Introit; Hymn; Prayer; Hymn or Lyric; The Ministry of the Word; The Old Testament; The Epistle; Te Deum; The Gospel Reading; Affirmation of Faith; Hymn; Sermon; Invitation to Christian Discipleship; Announcements; Tithes and Offertory; Hymn; and Benediction and Dismissal. Its relevance may be examined item by item. The Call to Worship is a way of calling the congregation's attention to the fact that the service is about to begin, after which the Choir, Singing Band and Clergy process; where the procession comes first, the liturgist may join the call to worship and welcome as one item after the introit. The Introit is sung in preparation for the continuation of the worship service after the procession by the choir. The Affirmation of Faith acts as a yardstick of correct belief, the Apostles' Creed being said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days, and by it Methodists affirm the doctrine of the Trinity. The place given to Lyrics helps to control the spontaneous singing of lyrics, while still allowing the preacher to accept those that are relevant to the sermon. The Response and Dedication, or altar call, is where people give or rededicate their lives to Christ, or seek corporate assistance in prayer, in response to the Word that has been preached, and is the appropriate time for ministry in healing, deliverance or the gifts of the Spirit, and for testimony sharing. The Dismissal with Blessing belongs to the clergy, and whenever a minister is present the local preacher must give him or her the first option to pronounce the benediction. Above all, the order of service is mainly a guideline: it is there to guide us in the conduct of worship but not to pin us down, and there should always be reasonable and cautious flexibility. The Te Deum, for instance, may be varied with other canticles, and a shorter canticle such as Canticle 6 may be sung where time must be saved, though some canticles are occasion specific — it is always appropriate to sing the Magnificat during Christmas.

subject: LIT
question: What is Pentecost? Examine the importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's Calendar.
idealAnswer: In Judaism, Pentecost was a harvest festival which was also known as the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of First Fruits. The descent of the Holy Spirit recorded in the Book of Acts took place at the Jewish Pentecost, and this made Christians fix their celebration of the pouring down of the Holy Spirit on the fiftieth day after Easter, that is, the seventh Sunday after Easter. It was a day of universal rejoicing, and as Tertullian records, “we spent our time in all exaltation”. The importance of Pentecost Sunday on the Church's calendar may be seen in several ways. St. Athanasius calls it “Magna Dominica”, the “Great Sunday”, and consequently neither fasting nor kneeling was allowed during its celebration. Pentecost Sunday is also called White Sunday or Whitsunday, possibly in reference to the white robes worn by catechumens and others who were baptised on that day; an alternative derivation is from the word “wit” or “wisdom”, which implies that it was the day the Apostles were filled with wisdom from God by the Holy Spirit. The sanctuary colour of Pentecost Sunday is red, the colour of the Church. The red symbolises the Fire of Pentecost as well as that of the Apostles and other disciples of Jesus who were gathered in the Upper Room for the empowerment from God to preach the gospel to other nations.

subject: LIT
question: Discuss a Textual Sermon and its advantages.
idealAnswer: In textual sermons the preacher takes a few verses, a verse, or even a part of a verse from the Bible. The preacher discovers the theme of the verse in context and preaches on it in his own words. In the textual sermon both the subject and the main points are based on ideas in the text, but, unlike the expository sermon, the development of the main ideas comes from sources outside of the immediate text. This sermon looks to the text to bring out the meaning, and uses the “hook-book-look-and-took” method: something is used to hook the audience, such as an interesting story; the book is turning to the Scripture; look discusses what that Scripture is saying; and the took is what each person should take away from the sermon. It is almost a combination of the narrative and expository sermons. A textual sermon is generally good for preaching to audiences with short attention spans such as children and the elderly, for preaching at occasions other than church services such as banquets and funerals, and for preaching series on “Great Bible Texts” or “Favourite Bible Verses”. Its advantages are these. First, a textual sermon is a great technique for bringing the actual words of the Bible before the hearers, giving Divine authority to the message. Secondly, since the text is short it will be easier to remember or memorise, so the preacher can easily make constant reference to the text many times during the sermon. Thirdly, the preacher who employs the textual method deals with distinctively Scriptural themes that come right out of the text, so that a well-constructed textual sermon is much more intimately in contact with the text, drawing from it not only the subject treated but all the leading thoughts of the treatment. Finally, it gives ample opportunity for variety, freshness and originality.
